title: User Access, Passwords, and Audit Trails

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe role-based access control and the principle of least privilege and explain how they limit access to protected health information.
- Apply password security practices, including creating strong passwords and never sharing credentials, to protect system access.
- Explain the purpose and content of audit trails and how logging access supports accountability and breach detection.
- Recognize the medical office assistant's role in following access policies, reporting security concerns, and escalating within scope of practice.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of a school: students get a key to their own locker, teachers get keys to the classrooms they teach in, and the principal gets more keys. Each person gets only the keys they need for their own job.

### Question 2

It is like lending your tools: you only hand a helper the one tool they need for their task, not the whole toolbox, so nothing gets used by mistake.

### Question 3

If you work the ticket counter at a movie theater, you need the ticket machine — not the keys to the projection room or the safe.

### Question 4

You would not give a friend your diary just because they said they were curious — being curious is not a good reason to look at someone's private information.

### Question 5

Like different keys in a building, access levels make sure people can only open the doors that are part of their own job.

### Question 6

When a new cashier starts, they get their own register code and drawer — not the keys to the whole store.

### Question 7

If someone grabs your house key, they get your whole house; but if they only grab a key to one cabinet, the damage is much smaller.

### Question 8

If you move from the art room to the music room, you trade in your art-room key for a music-room key instead of keeping both.

### Question 9

When someone moves away, you take back their key to the house so they can no longer walk in.

### Question 10

A chef gets knives, a driver gets car keys — the tools match the job, not who is friends with the boss.

### Question 11

If you notice a door is unlocked when it should be locked, you tell a grown-up in charge instead of walking through it yourself.

### Question 12

It is like a well-organized club where each member has a badge showing exactly which rooms they may enter.

### Question 13

A strong password is like a long, tricky secret code that is hard for someone else to figure out.

### Question 14

A strong password is like a long made-up sentence that only you know, not a single easy word someone could guess.

### Question 15

Pick a secret code that has nothing to do with your birthday or address, so no one can guess it from what they know about you.

### Question 16

Finding a password on a note is like finding a house key under the doormat — you should not use it; you should give it to the right person to keep safe.

### Question 17

Using your birthday in a code is like hiding your key in a spot everyone knows you would check first.

### Question 18

A temporary password is like a spare key the office gives you — you should get your own key made right away and keep it to yourself.

### Question 19

If you use the same key for your house, car, and locker, losing one key loses them all — different locks should have different keys.

### Question 20

A long secret sentence is harder to guess than one tiny word, just like a long combination lock is harder to open than a one-number lock.

### Question 21

A password manager is like a locked box that safely holds a different key for every door, so you only need to remember one way to open the box.

### Question 22

If you think someone saw your secret code, you change it right away instead of waiting to see if anything goes wrong.

### Question 23

It is like needing both a key and a special one-time code to open a door — even someone with the key cannot get in without the code.

### Question 24

It is like a door that asks for your key and then also sends a secret code to your phone before it opens.

### Question 25

Locking your screen is like locking your locker before you walk away, so no one else can open it while you are gone.

### Question 26

Before you leave a table with private papers, you put them away or cover them so no one else can read them.

### Question 27

Changing a secret code now and then is like changing a lock after a while, just in case someone figured out the old one.

### Question 28

A longer secret is like a longer lock combination — the more numbers there are, the harder it is to guess.

### Question 29

Your password is like your toothbrush — you never share it, no matter who asks.

### Question 30

If a friend's key breaks, you help them call a locksmith — you do not hand over your own key.

### Question 31

A unique login is like signing your own name on your work so everyone knows exactly who did what.

### Question 32

You sign your own name on your own work; you never sign someone else's name for them.

### Question 33

If a whole class shares one pencil, no one knows who wrote each answer on the test — that is the problem with shared accounts.

### Question 34

Even a visitor gets their own visitor badge with their own name, not a copy of the manager's badge.

### Question 35

It is like letting a friend take a test under your name — the teacher would not know who really answered.

### Question 36

If you lose your key, you get a new one made the proper way — you do not borrow your neighbor's key permanently.

### Question 37

If you find out someone used your name to get into a place they should not, you tell the person in charge and change your lock right away.

### Question 38

A unique login is like each player wearing their own number so the referee knows exactly who did what.

### Question 39

An audit trail is like a security camera log that writes down who opened each door and at what time.

### Question 40

Reviewing audit logs is like watching the security camera footage to see if anyone went somewhere they were not supposed to.

### Question 41

If a security camera shows someone opening a drawer they are not supposed to touch, you investigate — even if they did not take anything.

### Question 42

Audit controls are like keeping a careful logbook of everyone who uses the information system, so it can be checked later.

### Question 43

An audit trail is like a detailed diary of the day that you can read back to figure out exactly what happened and in what order.

### Question 44

It is normal for people to use the tools of their own job; what looks wrong is someone reaching into areas that are not part of their work.

### Question 45

An access log is like a sign-in sheet that records your name, what you did, and the time you did it.

### Question 46

To know what someone looked at, you check the camera log that recorded their every move in the system.

### Question 47

You never erase a security camera's footage just because it shows something embarrassing — the truth has to stay intact.

### Question 48

Checking the camera footage often helps you notice small problems before they turn into big ones.

### Question 49

It is like a sports scorebook that records who scored, what happened, and when — so you can look back at the whole game.

### Question 50

If your own logbook shows you 'signed in' when you were not there, someone else probably used your name — you would tell the person in charge.

### Question 51

People behave better when they know a camera is recording — the same idea applies to systems that log who opens what.

### Question 52

Even the best locks do not help if people leave the door open — training teaches everyone to use the locks properly.

### Question 53

You would not leave a private letter face-up on a public counter — you turn it over or put it where no one can read it.

### Question 54

An automatic logoff is like a door that locks itself if nobody touches it for a while.

### Question 55

A laptop with a lock and a secret code is like a diary with a lock — if it is lost, no one can open it.

### Question 56

Encryption is like locking a suitcase — if it is lost, no one can open it, but you still tell the person in charge that the suitcase is gone.

### Question 57

Both ideas are about the same habit: only taking the smallest amount of information you actually need for the task.

### Question 58

If you need one recipe, you open to that one page — you do not read the entire cookbook out loud.

### Question 59

Training is like teaching every player the rules of the game so everyone knows how to play safely and fairly.

### Question 60

You learn the safety rules before you start using the tools, not after something goes wrong.

### Question 61

Rules work when there are clear consequences — like how a class follows the rules better when the teacher consistently enforces them.

### Question 62

If a stranger emails asking for your secret code, you do not give it out — you tell a trusted adult in charge.

### Question 63

Phishing is like a fake friend pretending to be real, trying to get you to hand over your secret.

### Question 64

Before handing over a spare key, you first make sure the person really is who they say they are.

### Question 65

Shoulder surfing is like someone peeking at your answers during a test by looking over your shoulder.

### Question 66

Working with private files at home means using the safe, approved way the office provides — not any random connection.

### Question 67

If someone keeps trying the wrong key in a lock, the lock locks down for a while so they cannot keep guessing.

### Question 68

Authentication is proving you are you; authorization is deciding which doors you are allowed to open after that.

### Question 69

Multi-factor is like needing a key you have plus a code you know — two different kinds of proof, not two keys of the same kind.

### Question 70

Your fingerprint is something that is part of you, unlike a password you memorize or a badge you carry.

### Question 71

Give someone just the one key they need and only for the days they need it — not the whole key ring forever.

### Question 72

De-provisioning is like taking back someone's badge and keys when they leave so they cannot get back in.

### Question 73

An electronic system is like a door that automatically writes down everyone who walks through; a paper chart needs someone to write the sign-in by hand.

### Question 74

The camera log shows exactly who peeked at the famous visitor's file, even if no one admits it.

### Question 75

If you open the wrong door by accident, you close it and tell the person in charge instead of pretending it never happened.

### Question 76

When you only need a name and address, you look only at the name-and-address page — not the whole file.

### Question 77

To open the office files from far away, use the safe tunnel the office provides, not just any public door.

### Question 78

Least privilege means each person gets exactly the tools of their own job and nothing extra.

### Question 79

A secret written where everyone can see it is not a secret anymore.

### Question 80

Pick a secret sentence you can remember easily, like the words of a favorite made-up phrase, instead of writing a short code on paper.

### Question 81

The logbook will show normal, expected entries for real work — and anything unusual will stand out from them.

### Question 82

Once in a while you check the key box and take back any keys that should not still be out.

### Question 83

On a shared computer, everyone uses their own name and locks the door when they leave — no one shares one identity.

### Question 84

Encrypting is like putting a letter in a locked, coded envelope so only the right person can read it while it travels.

### Question 85

Protecting private information is like using a strong lock, giving each person their own key, and keeping a camera log — all at the same time.
